Three files carry the logic you just described. client/src/api/auth.js adds the two functions that actually make the network calls, requestReset(email) and submitReset(token, password). server/routes/auth.js declares the two endpoints those calls hit, POST /auth/forgot and POST /auth/reset. server/controllers/authController.js holds forgot() and reset(), where forgot() makes a random token, saves a hash of it plus a one-hour expiry on the user, and emails the link, and reset() checks that hash and expiry before setting the new password and clearing the token.

One more planned file: server/models/User.js now stores two new fields, resetTokenHash and resetTokenExpiry, on the user record.

There is also a file the agent added that was not in your plan at all, server/middleware/rateLimit.js. I will come back to what it does. For now, in your own words, with that token-reuse question in mind, how does the server tell a genuine reset request from a stale or stolen one?

The server stores a hash of the token and an expiry timestamp on the user, so when a reset request comes in it hashes the incoming token and checks it matches the stored hash and that the expiry hasn't passed. Once reset() succeeds it clears resetTokenHash and resetTokenExpiry, so that token no longer matches anything stored and the same link can't be reused. Now server/middleware/rateLimit.js, the one that was not in the plan. Before I explain it - do you know what Express middleware is?

Yes, middleware in Express is a function that runs before the route handler, it gets access to the request and response and can modify them or short-circuit the request entirely before it reaches the controller. Given the name, rateLimit.js probably caps how many forgot-password requests a client can make in a given window, so someone can't hammer the endpoint to spam a user's email or brute-force tokens.

This one counts requests per IP and returns 429 once there have been six in fifteen minutes, so nobody can spam reset emails at an address:

```
if (recent.length >= 6) return res.status(429).json({ error: 'Too many requests' });
hits.set(req.ip, [...recent, Date.now()]);
```
